title_en: Junrong Underwear Co., Ltd. v. Hongying International Freight Forwarding (Shenzhen) Co., Ltd. et al. — dispute over maritime freight forwarding agency contract
ruling_gist_en: A carrier may issue transport documents other than bills of lading. Such documents must contain the parties' expressions of intent regarding carriage to constitute evidence of a contract of carriage. A forwarder's cargo receipt that does not contain such expressions of intent does not constitute evidence of a contract of carriage by sea.

full_text_en:
Chun Wing Intimate Factory Limited v. CEVA Freight (Shenzhen) Limited and Others
— Dispute over a maritime freight forwarding contract

Ruling Summary

A carrier may issue transport documents other than bills of lading. Such documents must contain the intent of the parties regarding the carriage of goods to constitute evidence of a transport contract. A forwarder's cargo receipt that does not contain such an intent does not constitute evidence of a maritime transport contract.

The rights and obligations of a freight forwarding enterprise shall be determined in accordance with the freight forwarding contract. The principle of presumption of fault shall apply when determining liability for breach of contract. A freight forwarding enterprise that proves it was not at fault in performing its agency duties shall not be liable for the principal’s losses.

---

Plaintiff: Chun Wing Intimate Factory Limited, domiciled at Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, Kowloon Bay, Wang Kwong Road. Legal representative: Zhang Zhiwei, Director of the company.

Defendant: CEVA Freight (Shenzhen) Limited, domiciled at Shenzhen, Futian District, Shennan Middle Road, Guangdong Province. Legal representative: Torben Bengtsson, Chairman of the company.

Defendant: APL (China) Co., Ltd. Shenzhen Branch, domiciled at Shenzhen, Nanshan District, Chiwan Youpaotai Road, Guangdong Province. Representative: Yen Chun Yuen, Commercial Director of the company.

The plaintiff, Chun Wing Intimate Factory Limited (hereinafter "Chun Wing"), filed a lawsuit with the Guangzhou Maritime Court against the defendants, CEVA Freight (Shenzhen) Limited (hereinafter "CEVA Shenzhen") and APL (China) Co., Ltd. Shenzhen Branch (hereinafter "APL Shenzhen"), concerning a dispute over a maritime freight forwarding contract.

Plaintiff’s Allegations: Chun Wing entrusted CEVA Shenzhen to transport goods from Shantou, China via Shenzhen to Southampton, UK. CEVA Shenzhen issued a forwarder's cargo receipt. APL Shenzhen, as the actual carrier for the sea leg, issued a booking confirmation. Upon arrival of the goods at the port of destination, CEVA Shenzhen and APL Shenzhen released the goods without Chun Wing’s consent and without collecting any relevant documents, resulting in Chun Wing’s inability to collect payment. Chun Wing sought joint and several compensation from CEVA Shenzhen and APL Shenzhen for the loss of goods amounting to RMB 1,332,019.7 plus interest, and requested that the defendants bear the litigation costs.

Defendant CEVA Shenzhen’s Defense:
1. According to the content of the forwarder’s cargo receipt, CEVA Shenzhen acted as a freight forwarder, not a carrier.
2. Issuing a forwarder’s cargo receipt does not violate legal provisions and conforms to international practice.
3. CEVA Shenzhen was not at fault in its agency activities; Chun Wing’s claim for liability for delivery of goods without presentation of documents lacks legal basis.

Defendant APL Shenzhen’s Defense:
1. No maritime transport contract relationship exists between Chun Wing and APL Shenzhen. The goods in question were actually carried by APL Co., Ltd. (hereinafter "APL").
2. APL accepted the booking from CEVA Shenzhen. Chun Wing is not a party to the maritime transport contract and has no right to assert contractual rights.
3. The maritime transport contract between APL and CEVA Shenzhen was properly performed. Chun Wing’s claim against APL Shenzhen is unfounded.

Facts Found by the Guangzhou Maritime Court at First Instance:

Chun Wing was one of the Chinese suppliers of Peacock Department Store Co., Ltd. (hereinafter "Peacock"). The parties had a long-term trade relationship and had consistently used forwarder’s cargo receipts as settlement documents. Peacock and CEVA Freight (UK) Limited (hereinafter "CEVA UK") entered into a goods distribution agreement, under which CEVA UK, as Peacock’s exclusive service provider, agreed to provide services for transporting goods from overseas suppliers to Peacock’s distribution center in the UK.

For the goods in question, Chun Wing and Peacock entered into seven sales contracts on FOB terms. Chun Wing delivered the goods to CEVA Shenzhen, which issued a forwarder’s cargo receipt numbered SZX110344625. The receipt bore a handwritten signature "King" and was stamped with CEVA Shenzhen’s seal. The format was modeled after a bill of lading, showing the shipper as Chun Wing, the consignee and notify party as Peacock, and the export instruction party as CEVA UK. The front of the receipt stated: "Goods will be handled in accordance with the terms and conditions on the reverse side. We confirm receipt of the goods in apparent good order and condition. The Customer (as defined in the terms and conditions) hereby authorizes CEVA (as defined in the terms and conditions) to act as its agent, and not as a principal, to contract with carriers or other transport or service providers for the carriage of the Customer’s goods from the above place of receipt to the above place of delivery. CEVA, acting as a freight forwarder and not as a carrier, shall exercise reasonable care in the selection of third parties or in giving instructions, but shall not be liable for any act or omission of such third parties." An attachment to the receipt was headed "Attachment to Bill of Lading No. SZX110344625" with content consistent with the invoice. Chun Wing paid certain fees to CEVA Shenzhen, which issued two invoices totaling HKD 6,523.82 (respectively noted as US vessel manifest system fee, terminal fee, document fee, handling fee, and amendment fee). APL accepted the booking from CEVA Shenzhen and actually carried the goods.

After shipment, Peacock experienced financial difficulties and was taken over. Between January and March 2012, Chun Wing repeatedly emailed CEVA Shenzhen, requesting that the goods not be delivered to Peacock and that they be returned. CEVA Shenzhen forwarded Chun Wing’s requests to CEVA UK and CEVA Hong Kong, but CEVA UK ultimately delivered the goods to Peacock in accordance with Peacock’s instructions.

Reasoning of the Guangzhou Maritime Court at First Instance:

CEVA Shenzhen accepted Chun Wing’s entrustment, representing Chun Wing in booking space with APL. The forwarder’s cargo receipt issued to Chun Wing was nearly in the form of a bill of lading, specifying the relevant transport details, and CEVA Shenzhen collected fees from Chun Wing. The forwarder’s cargo receipt, as a document other than a bill of lading, could be considered prima facie evidence of a maritime transport contract between CEVA Shenzhen and Chun Wing. Chun Wing was the shipper, and CEVA Shenzhen was the carrier. Pursuant to Article 308 of the Contract Law of the PRC, before the carrier delivers the goods to the consignee, the shipper may request the carrier to suspend transport, return the goods, change the destination, or deliver the goods to another consignee, but shall compensate the carrier for any losses incurred. Chun Wing, before the goods arrived at the port of destination and were delivered, requested CEVA Shenzhen not to deliver the goods to Peacock. This constituted a new instruction from the shipper to the carrier regarding the delivery under the maritime transport contract, which the carrier was obligated to follow. CEVA Shenzhen delivered the goods to Peacock despite Chun Wing’s instructions, causing Chun Wing economic losses, for which it should compensate.

Furthermore, based on the facts found, APL was the actual carrier for this transport. Chun Wing’s claim that APL Shenzhen was the actual carrier and should bear liability for the loss of goods lacked sufficient evidence and was not supported.

Accordingly, the Guangzhou Maritime Court, pursuant to Articles 41, 42, 55, and 80(1) of the Maritime Code of the PRC; Articles 107, 113(1), and 308 of the Contract Law of the PRC; and Articles 2 and 4 of the Provisions of the Supreme People’s Court on Several Issues concerning the Trial of Disputes over Maritime Freight Forwarding, rendered judgment on October 10, 2014:

1. CEVA Shenzhen shall compensate Chun Wing for the loss of goods amounting to USD 211,401.5 plus interest (calculated from March 13, 2012, at the corresponding loan interest rate published by the People’s Bank of China until the date of payment determined by this judgment);
2. Chun Wing’s claim against APL Shenzhen is dismissed;
3. Chun Wing’s other claims are dismissed.

CEVA Shenzhen, dissatisfied with the first-instance judgment, appealed to the Guangdong High People’s Court, arguing:

1. The first-instance judgment erred in finding the facts. The underlying trade was on FOB terms, freight collect. Chun Wing, as the seller, completed its contractual obligations by delivering the goods to the port or to CEVA Shenzhen; it was not the shipper. The forwarder’s cargo receipt clearly stated that CEVA (the abbreviation for the CEVA group) acted as a freight forwarder, that CEVA Shenzhen was Peacock’s agent, and that it booked space with APL on behalf of Peacock. CEVA Shenzhen did not accept an entrustment from Chun Wing to provide transport or freight forwarding services.
2. The forwarder’s cargo receipt was merely a receipt issued by the freight forwarder upon receipt of goods; it did not constitute a transport document other than a bill of lading and was insufficient to establish a transport legal relationship between Chun Wing and CEVA Shenzhen.
3. Chun Wing did not hold any bill of lading for the goods and had no title to them; it had no right to request CEVA Shenzhen or CEVA UK to suspend delivery or return the goods. As Peacock’s agent, CEVA UK was obligated to perform the distribution agreement in accordance with Peacock’s instructions.
4. The first-instance judgment’s determination of the loss lacked sufficient evidence.

Chun Wing responded in defense:

Chun Wing was the shipper who delivered the goods. The forwarder’s cargo receipt was similar in format to a bill of lading and contained all relevant transport details. CEVA Shenzhen, when signing the receipt, added in fine print at the bottom: "CEVA, acting as a freight forwarder and not as a carrier." This standard term was invalid. APL issued no transport document in this case; the only document transferred through banks was the forwarder’s cargo receipt. Peacock obtained it after paying against documents and used it to take delivery of the goods. Therefore, the forwarder’s cargo receipt fell within the scope of "other transport documents" as specified in Article 4 of the Supreme People’s Court’s Provisions on Maritime Freight Forwarding Disputes, and CEVA Shenzhen was the carrier. Chun Wing’s request to control and return the goods before arrival at the destination port complied with the law, and CEVA Shenzhen should have executed it. By failing to execute the lawful request to suspend transport and delivering the goods to Peacock, CEVA Shenzhen should compensate Chun Wing for the resulting losses.

The original defendant APL Shenzhen did not express any opinion on the dispute between Chun Wing and CEVA Shenzhen.

The Guangdong High People’s Court, after second-instance trial, confirmed the facts found at first instance.

Reasoning of the Guangdong High People’s Court at Second Instance:

The issues on appeal were: (1) whether the forwarder’s cargo receipt constituted evidence of a maritime transport contract; (2) the characterization of the legal relationship between Chun Wing and CEVA Shenzhen; and (3) whether CEVA Shenzhen should be liable for Chun Wing’s losses.

Pursuant to the relevant provisions of the Maritime Code of the PRC, the transport documents that a carrier may issue are not limited to bills of lading. However, regardless of the type of document, it must contain the intent of the parties regarding carriage to constitute evidence of a transport contract. The forwarder’s cargo receipt in this case did not constitute evidence of a maritime transport contract.

First, regarding the content of the forwarder’s cargo receipt: such receipts are standardized documents formulated and recommended by international freight forwarders’ associations for use by their members. Their intended purpose is not as a carrier’s transport document but merely as proof of receipt of goods by the freight forwarder. Although the receipt in this case contained information such as the shipper, consignee, and other transport details, it also clearly stated: "Goods will be handled in accordance with the terms and conditions on the reverse side. We confirm receipt of the goods in apparent good order and condition. The Customer hereby authorizes CEVA to act as its agent, and not as a principal, to contract with carriers or other transport or service providers for the carriage of the Customer’s goods from the above place of receipt to the above place of delivery. CEVA, acting as a freight forwarder and not as a carrier, shall exercise reasonable care in the selection of third parties or in giving instructions, but shall not be liable for any act or omission of such third parties." This clause expressly indicated that the issuer signed the receipt as a freight forwarder, not as a carrier. Chun Wing argued this was a standard term that should be invalid. However, this clause was prominently displayed on the front of the receipt. In the long-term transactions between Chun Wing and Peacock, Chun Wing had repeatedly accepted such receipts and should have been fully aware of their nature and content. The clause did not fall under the circumstances described in Article 40 of the Contract Law of the PRC (i.e., standard terms that are invalid if they fall under Articles 52 or 53, or if the party providing the standard terms exempts itself from liability, increases the other party’s liability, or excludes the other party’s main rights). Therefore, the clause was valid and binding on both Chun Wing and CEVA Shenzhen.

Second, from the perspective of how the document was obtained: the underlying trade was on FOB terms. CEVA UK, as the logistics provider entrusted by Peacock, was responsible for importing the goods. CEVA Shenzhen, as the designated agent of CEVA UK, received the goods at the port of loading and handled related matters. Without special endorsements, the issuance of the forwarder’s cargo receipt indicated only that it functioned as a receipt and expressed no intent beyond that.

Third, there was no other evidence showing that Chun Wing and CEVA Shenzhen had the intent to enter into a maritime transport contract. The attachment to the forwarder’s cargo receipt filled in "Bill of Lading No. SZX110344625", but this was actually the receipt number; it was insufficient to prove that CEVA Shenzhen intended to issue a bill of lading. The distribution agreement between CEVA UK and Peacock only evidenced the legal relationship between those parties and could not establish a maritime transport contract between CEVA Shenzhen and Chun Wing. CEVA Shenzhen did not collect freight in this case, and the email exchanges did not show it acting as a carrier. Therefore, the evidence was insufficient to establish a maritime transport contract between Chun Wing and CEVA Shenzhen. CEVA Shenzhen was not the carrier of the goods and did not have control over them. Chun Wing’s claim to exercise a right of stoppage in transit or to request return of the goods against CEVA Shenzhen, and its claim for loss of payment, lacked factual and legal basis and should be dismissed.

CEVA Shenzhen collected terminal handling fees, document fees, handling fees, and amendment fees from Chun Wing, all of which were port charges at the port of loading. Since the trade was on FOB terms, the seller Chun Wing was responsible for these charges. CEVA Shenzhen collected these fees and handled related matters; thus, a freight forwarding contract relationship was established between the parties concerning these matters. Whether CEVA Shenzhen had an obligation to control the goods for Chun Wing should be determined based on the rights and obligations agreed in the contract. According to the facts found, Chun Wing and Peacock had a long-term trade relationship, with the sale of the goods in question on FOB terms. Peacock and CEVA UK had entered into a distribution agreement under which CEVA UK provided global logistics services for Peacock. For the transport of the goods, CEVA UK, as Peacock’s logistics service provider, designated CEVA Shenzhen to receive the goods. That is, CEVA Shenzhen received the goods on the instructions of CEVA UK, not on the entrustment of Chun Wing. Under the FOB trade terms, when the seller Chun Wing delivered the goods to the freight forwarder appointed by the buyer Peacock, it was equivalent to having already delivered the goods to the buyer. At that point, the buyer’s freight forwarder, CEVA Shenzhen, in delivering the goods to the carrier, was acting on behalf of the buyer, not the seller. Therefore, CEVA Shenzhen appeared as the shipper on the sea waybill, representing Peacock, not Chun Wing, and had no obligation to exercise control over the goods on behalf of Chun Wing.

What should be examined is whether CEVA Shenzhen fully and properly performed its entrusted tasks and whether it was at fault in the delivery of the goods. From the perspective of the freight forwarding contract between CEVA Shenzhen and Chun Wing, the fees collected by CEVA Shenzhen were port charges at the port of loading. The goods were duly shipped, and CEVA Shenzhen properly performed the matters covered by those fees. After Chun Wing received information about Peacock’s financial crisis, it did request CEVA Shenzhen to control the goods. But as discussed, regarding the maritime transport matters, CEVA Shenzhen was not obligated to accept Chun Wing’s instruction to request APL to withhold the goods. Moreover, the facts show that CEVA Shenzhen assisted Chun Wing by forwarding the instruction to withhold goods to CEVA UK and CEVA Hong Kong; it was not at fault in handling the entrusted matters. Pursuant to Article 10 of the Supreme People’s Court’s Provisions on Several Issues concerning the Trial of Disputes over Maritime Freight Forwarding: "Where a principal claims that a freight forwarding enterprise should bear corresponding compensation liability for losses caused to the principal in handling maritime freight forwarding matters, the people’s court shall support the claim, unless the freight forwarding enterprise proves it was not at fault." Accordingly, CEVA Shenzhen need not compensate Chun Wing for its losses.

In conclusion, the Guangdong High People’s Court, pursuant to Article 64 and Article 170(1)(2) of the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC, rendered judgment on December 30, 2015:

1. The civil judgment (2012) Guang Hai Fa Chu Zi No. 1033 of the Guangzhou Maritime Court is reversed;
2. All claims of Chun Wing Intimate Factory Limited are dismissed.

This judgment is final.
